key_insight: An octopus-inspired soft arm embeds optoelectronic mechanosensors in its suction cups to perform local (peripheral) inference of contact and object position, enabling robust autonomous underwater grasping without heavy centralized perception.
problem_solved: Underwater manipulation is hard due to poor visibility, compliance of soft bodies, and the latency/complexity of centralized sensing and control. This work shows how distributed, local sensing can close the loop at the periphery to achieve reliable grasping in challenging aquatic environments.
method: Bioinspired soft arm with integrated optoelectronic mechanosensors in each suction cup to transduce contact/force signals.
Peripheral inference pipeline that interprets local sensor signals to estimate contact location and trigger local grasp control, reducing dependence on central perception.
Experimental validation in underwater grasping tasks comparing performance (e.g., success rate, responsiveness) with centralized baselines.
impact: Demonstrates a practical route to decentralize perception and control in robotic systems—useful for ML practitioners designing edge inference, sensor-fusion, and control policies for soft and constrained environments. It reduces data/compute load on central systems and improves robustness and responsiveness.
visual_elements: Annotated illustration of the octopus-inspired soft arm with labeled suction-cup sensors and actuator segments.
Close-up schematic of an optoelectronic mechanosensor showing sensing principle and signal output.
Pipeline diagram: distributed sensors → peripheral inference (local processing) → local actuation / grasp decision.
Comparative chart (e.g., grasp success rate, latency) showing distributed/peripheral approach vs centralized baseline.
paper_title: Peripheral control enabled by distributed sensing in an octopus-inspired soft robotic arm for autonomous underwater grasping
paper_authors: Emanuela Del Dottore, Romina Adhami, Ebrahim Shahabi, Emanuele Solfiti, Michele Martini
